Isole di calore urbane: quando il caldo trasforma le città

Più alberi, più suolo naturale, meno superfici che accumulano calore e una progettazione urbana basata sui dati possono trasformare il modo in cui le città affrontano le ondate di calore

Foto di Rogerio Rogeriomda su Pixabay
                                            
                
                
                    L’estate 2026 sta mettendo sotto pressione città e territori italiani con una successione di ondate di calore particolarmente persistenti. I dati raccontano una stagione nella quale non sono soltanto i picchi termici a destare preoccupazione, ma soprattutto la loro durata e la difficoltà delle temperature a scendere durante la notte.
In Toscana il quadro è particolarmente significativo. Secondo il Consorzio LaMMA, luglio 2026 è stato il mese più caldo mai registrato in Toscana dall’inizio della serie nel 1955, probabilmente anche rispetto ai secoli precedenti. Il bimestre giugno-luglio si colloca invece al secondo posto nella serie storica, alle spalle del 2003. La temperatura media regionale nei due mesi è stata di 25,6 °C, contro i 26,2 °C del 2003. Ancora più indicativi sono i dati relativi a Firenze: nel periodo considerato le temperature hanno superato i 36 °C in 27 giorni, mentre altrettante sono state le notti tropicali, con temperature minime mai inferiori a 20 °C. La persistenza del caldo è un elemento particolarmente importante perché l’assenza di un adeguato raffrescamento notturno aumenta gli effetti sulla salute e sulla vivibilità degli ambienti urbani. 
È proprio in questo scenario che il fenomeno delle isole di calore urbane diventa particolarmente rilevante.
Che cos’è un’isola di calore urbana
L’isola di calore urbana, o Urban Heat Island (UHI), è il fenomeno per cui le aree urbanizzate possono raggiungere temperature superiori rispetto alle zone rurali o meno densamente costruite circostanti. Non si tratta semplicemente del fatto che in città “faccia più caldo”. È il risultato dell’interazione fra atmosfera, materiali, geometria urbana, vegetazione, disponibilità d’acqua e attività umane. L’ambiente costruito modifica, infatti, il bilancio energetico della superficie: asfalto, cemento e altri materiali artificiali assorbono la radiazione solare durante il giorno e possono restituire lentamente il calore accumulato, contribuendo a mantenere temperature elevate anche dopo il tramonto.
Il fenomeno non interessa soltanto i centri cittadini più compatti: esistono veri e propri “arcipelaghi di calore”, con zone ad alto rischio anche nelle aree periferiche.
Uno degli aspetti più importanti è la distribuzione spaziale del calore. Due quartieri della stessa città possono avere condizioni molto diverse: uno caratterizzato da alberature, suoli permeabili e spazi verdi può risultare sensibilmente più fresco di un’area dominata da superfici impermeabili, edifici e parcheggi.
L’intensità dell’isola di calore dipende da numerosi fattori.

Copertura del suolo. Cemento, asfalto e altre superfici impermeabili modificano il modo in cui l’energia solare viene assorbita e restituita all’ambiente. Al contrario, suoli naturali e vegetazione favoriscono processi che sottraggono energia al riscaldamento della superficie.
Presenza di alberi e vegetazione. Le chiome producono ombra e la vegetazione contribuisce al raffrescamento attraverso l’evapotraspirazione. Non basta però considerare soltanto la quantità di verde: anche la sua disposizione, le specie utilizzate, la disponibilità idrica e le condizioni del suolo sono importanti.
Forma della città. Altezza e disposizione degli edifici, larghezza delle strade, orientamento degli isolati e densità edilizia influenzano la circolazione dell’aria, l’esposizione alla radiazione solare e la capacità degli spazi urbani di disperdere il calore.
Attività antropiche, comprese le emissioni di calore associate ai trasporti, agli edifici e agli impianti di climatizzazione.
Condizioni meteorologiche: vento, umidità, radiazione solare e persistenza delle alte pressioni possono amplificare o attenuare il fenomeno.

Logo del progetto Mirificus
MIRIFICUS: dai satelliti alla progettazione delle città
È importante distinguere fra UHI atmosferica e Surface Urban Heat Island (SUHI). Quest’ultima riguarda in particolare la temperatura delle superfici urbane, osservabile attraverso i satelliti. È proprio sulla SUHI che si concentra MIRIFICUS – Monitoraggio degli Interventi di RIForestazione per l’Isola di Calore Urbana tramite i Satelliti.
Il progetto, coordinato dal CNR-IBE con la partecipazione di ISPRA e il coinvolgimento di ANCI e dei Comuni di Roma e Firenze, utilizza dati satellitari per analizzare la distribuzione degli elementi urbani che influenzano l’isola di calore e per valutare l’efficacia degli interventi di riforestazione.
Il progetto combina dati provenienti da diversi satelliti: Sentinel 1 e 2 per la copertura e il consumo del suolo e Landsat 8, Landsat 9 e MODIS per l’andamento della temperatura superficiale. L’analisi copre il periodo 2013-2023 e viene sviluppata sia a scala nazionale sia a scala comunale. Per Roma e Firenze sono state inoltre realizzate simulazioni microclimatiche finalizzate a valutare l’efficacia di ipotetici interventi di riforestazione urbana.
L’obiettivo non è quindi soltanto fotografare dove si concentra il caldo, ma individuare le aree più esposte, simulare possibili interventi e fornire alle amministrazioni informazioni per decidere dove e come intervenire.
Firenze come laboratorio
I risultati presentati nel 2026 mostrano quanto questa impostazione possa essere concreta: nelle simulazioni realizzate nell’area Mercafir/Piazza Artom a Firenze, la combinazione di nuove alberature, nuovi spazi verdi e superfici capaci di accumulare meno calore produce una riduzione della temperatura superiore a 4 °C nelle ore comprese fra le 9 e le 15. La diminuzione resta intorno a 2-2,2 °C considerando la media giornaliera.
Firenze rappresenta quindi uno dei casi più interessanti per comprendere il rapporto fra caldo estremo e struttura urbana. La città arriva all’estate 2026 dopo una sequenza di temperature elevate e notti tropicali che rendono particolarmente importante la capacità degli spazi urbani di raffrescarsi. I dati MIRIFICUS mostrano che all’interno del territorio comunale il comportamento termico non è uniforme.
Nell’analisi del progetto, le aree caratterizzate da edifici compatti di media altezza possono raggiungere temperature superficiali estive molto elevate: per Firenze viene indicato un valore di 44,6 °C. Nelle aree con boschi urbani, invece, il valore scende fino a 35,9 °C. Si tratta di una differenza prossima ai 9 °C, che mostra con particolare evidenza il ruolo della struttura e della copertura del suolo nel determinare il microclima urbano.
Il dato non significa che piantare alberi produca automaticamente una riduzione di nove gradi in qualsiasi strada o quartiere: le temperature citate si riferiscono a differenti tipologie urbane individuate dall’analisi. È però una dimostrazione molto efficace di quanto possa essere ampia la differenza termica fra superfici e configurazioni urbane diverse.
Il caso Mercafir-Piazza Artom è ancora più significativo perché permette di passare dall’osservazione alla simulazione di un intervento. Qui MIRIFICUS ha valutato uno scenario nel quale alberature, spazi verdi e superfici meno inclini ad accumulare calore vengono combinati all’interno dell’area urbana. Il risultato simulato è una riduzione superiore ai 4 °C nelle ore centrali della giornata.
Non solo più alberi: progettare il raffrescamento urbano
Il messaggio che emerge da MIRIFICUS è più articolato del semplice invito a “piantare alberi”. La vegetazione deve essere progettata come una vera infrastruttura urbana, tenendo conto del microclima, del tipo di suolo, della disponibilità d’acqua, dell’ombreggiamento e della ventilazione. Anche scelta delle specie e manutenzione sono elementi essenziali. La strategia di adattamento, dunque, non può limitarsi alla forestazione. Deve comprendere la depavimentazione, la restituzione di suolo naturale, l’aumento degli spazi verdi, l’ombreggiamento, la scelta di materiali e superfici che accumulino meno calore e una progettazione urbana capace di favorire la ventilazione.
Il valore del progetto MIRIFICUS sta proprio nella possibilità di mettere in relazione le scelte con dati misurabili. Il WebGIS consente di confrontare temperatura superficiale, consumo di suolo e presenza di verde e di individuare le aree nelle quali gli interventi possono essere più efficaci. I satelliti permettono oggi di osservare il territorio con un livello di dettaglio che fino a pochi anni fa sarebbe stato difficile da ottenere su scala nazionale. MIRIFICUS utilizza queste informazioni per costruire una fotografia delle temperature superficiali e delle caratteristiche urbane e per arrivare, nei casi studio, alla simulazione di possibili interventi.
Foto di StockSnap su Pixabay
Rifugi climatici: una rete di luoghi per affrontare il caldo
Se la riforestazione urbana e la depavimentazione agiscono sulle cause e sulle condizioni che amplificano il calore in città, i rifugi climatici rappresentano una risposta più immediata: sono luoghi nei quali le persone possono trovare sollievo durante le ore più calde e, soprattutto, durante le ondate di calore. Spazi pubblici, o comunque accessibili alla popolazione, nei quali siano disponibili condizioni più favorevoli rispetto all’ambiente urbano circostante: ombra, acqua potabile, ambienti freschi o climatizzati, possibilità di sedersi e ripararsi dal caldo. Possono essere biblioteche, centri civici, strutture sanitarie, parchi alberati, giardini, musei o altri spazi pubblici.
La loro funzione è duplice:

offrono un luogo di sollievo termico alle persone che vivono o si spostano in città;
costituiscono uno strumento di protezione della salute pubblica, particolarmente importante per anziani, bambini, persone fragili e per chi vive in abitazioni difficili da raffrescare. La stessa Organizzazione Mondiale della Sanità considera l’apertura di rifugi climatici una delle possibili misure da attivare durante le ondate di calore, prevedendo, quando necessario, anche forme di trasporto per le persone più vulnerabili.

Un rifugio climatico, tuttavia, non deve essere considerato come una soluzione alternativa alla trasformazione della città. È piuttosto un elemento di una strategia più ampia. Da un lato servono interventi strutturali — più alberi, suoli permeabili, ombra, superfici meno inclini ad accumulare calore, edifici meglio progettati — capaci di ridurre l’isola di calore; dall’altro è necessario mettere a disposizione una rete di luoghi freschi e facilmente raggiungibili che permetta alle persone di proteggersi quando il caldo raggiunge livelli pericolosi.
È importante, inoltre, che questi luoghi siano distribuiti in modo capillare e accessibili senza costi. Un rifugio climatico molto lontano dal quartiere di residenza, difficile da raggiungere a piedi o privo di informazioni chiare sulla sua disponibilità rischia infatti di essere poco utile proprio alle persone che ne hanno maggiore necessità. La disponibilità di acqua e l’accessibilità sono considerate elementi importanti anche nelle strategie europee di adattamento al calore urbano.
La Toscana offre già alcuni esempi concreti di questa strategia. Il caso più strutturato è quello di Firenze, dove il Comune ha aggiornato nel luglio 2026 la propria rete portandola a 53 rifugi climatici, la rete comprende biblioteche, parchi e giardini ombreggiati e, dal 2026, anche alcune sedi dei quartieri. Tra i criteri considerati figurano la presenza di ombreggiatura, acqua potabile e, per gli spazi al chiuso, la possibilità di usufruire di ambienti climatizzati. Il Comune mette inoltre a disposizione una mappa interattiva, attraverso la quale è possibile conoscere le caratteristiche dei singoli luoghi, compresa la percentuale di ombreggiamento di parchi e giardini e la posizione dei fontanelli.
L’esperienza fiorentina è particolarmente interessante perché mette in relazione il concetto di rifugio climatico con quello di infrastruttura verde. I rifugi non sono pensati soltanto come luoghi nei quali “scappare” dal caldo, ma fanno parte di una strategia più ampia che comprende l’aumento della copertura arborea, la creazione di aree ombreggiate, la depavimentazione di parchi e giardini e l’impiego di superfici capaci di riflettere maggiormente la radiazione solare.
Firenze non è però l’unico esempio toscano. A Livorno è stata predisposta una rete molto ampia, con oltre un centinaio di luoghi individuati tra biblioteche, musei, chiese, parchi e sedi comunali. L’obiettivo non è soltanto offrire un riparo durante le giornate più calde, ma anche aumentare la consapevolezza della popolazione sui rischi legati al cambiamento climatico e creare una base per una pianificazione urbana maggiormente orientata all’adattamento. Anche Prato ha adottato questo approccio, individuando sette rifugi climatici all’interno di strutture pubbliche già esistenti, tra cui biblioteche, il Centro per l’arte contemporanea Luigi Pecci e il Museo di Palazzo Pretorio.
Queste esperienze mostrano un aspetto importante: il rifugio climatico non richiede necessariamente la costruzione di nuove infrastrutture. In molti casi è possibile adattare e mettere in rete luoghi che la città possiede già, rendendoli riconoscibili, accessibili e utilizzabili nei periodi di caldo estremo.
Il concetto di rifugio climatico completa quindi quello di isola di calore urbana. Se MIRIFICUS permette di individuare le aree nelle quali il territorio urbano tende a surriscaldarsi e di simulare gli effetti di interventi come la riforestazione e la depavimentazione, la rete dei rifugi climatici può fornire una risposta concreta alla popolazione nelle fasi di maggiore emergenza.
La prospettiva più efficace è quella di mettere insieme le due strategie. Una città resiliente al caldo deve avere sia meno superfici che accumulano calore sia più luoghi nei quali le persone possano trovare sollievo quando il caldo diventa estremo, presidi di prossimità contro il rischio climatico, inseriti nella vita quotidiana della città e attivabili nei momenti in cui le condizioni meteorologiche diventano più pericolose.
La sfida, in definitiva, è costruire una città nella quale non sia necessario scegliere tra scappare dal caldo e trasformare la città. Le due cose devono procedere insieme: i rifugi climatici proteggono oggi, mentre alberi, suoli permeabili, depavimentazioni e una progettazione urbana più attenta al microclima contribuiscono a rendere la città meno vulnerabile domani.

Limiting warming by CO2 and methane mitigation in an expanded scenario space
                        Konstantin Weber 
            ORCID: orcid.org/0009-0003-5230-02831, Reto Knutti 
            ORCID: orcid.org/0000-0001-8303-67001, Lena Brun 
            ORCID: orcid.org/0009-0004-5710-25311 & …Cyril Brunner 
            ORCID: orcid.org/0000-0001-8280-42531 Show authors

Communications Earth & Environment

AbstractAnthropogenic methane (CH4) currently contributes more than 0.6 ∘C to global warming, and CH4 mitigation is a powerful option to limit near-term warming. Assessments of greenhouse gas (GHG) mitigation rely on Integrated Assessment Model scenarios with typically non-linear emission trajectories (due to economic optimization) and similar mitigation ambition for CO2 and CH4. However, climate targets are often linear and focused primarily on CO2. Here, we present a complementary scenario generation approach to systematically map peak warming resulting from two political choices: the net zero emissions year for CO2 or GHG after linear reductions, and the simultaneous change in CH4 emissions. We show that without CH4 mitigation, peak warming exceeds 1.7 ∘C (50% likelihood), and the likelihood of keeping warming below 2 ∘C drops below 50% with net zero CO2 emissions after 2050. Irrespective of CH4 mitigation stringency, limiting warming to 1.5 ∘C is no longer plausible. An additional sustained linear 10% reduction in CH4 emissions ( ~ 35 MtCH4/year) until 2050 increases the 2 ∘C-compatible remaining carbon budget by  ~ 165 GtCO2. These results emphasize the benefit of near-term CH4 mitigation.

IntroductionTo limit global temperature rise to a specific level, global society needs to reach net zero CO2 emissions and strongly reduce non-CO2 greenhouse gas (GHG) emissions1. Methane (CH4) is the most important non-CO2 GHG, contributing about 0.6 ∘C to global warming until 20252. CO2 and CH4 behave fundamentally differently: CO2-induced warming is proportional to cumulative CO2 emissions3,4,5. This provides the scientific basis for net zero or near zero CO2 emissions to halt global warming6,7,8 and a finite global remaining carbon budget5,9,10 (RCB) to limit warming to specific levels. In contrast, CH4 has a mean atmospheric lifetime of around 9 years11,12, making CH4-induced warming transient and largely dependent on recent emissions13. Reducing anthropogenic CH4 emissions thus slows warming on policy-relevant time scales14,15.Strong CH4 mitigation is needed to achieve set climate targets16,17, and there is high CH4 mitigation potential12,15,18,19. Considering currently available measures, the UNEP Global Methane Status Report20 estimates that combining decarbonization with maximum technically feasible reductions could lower anthropogenic CH4 emissions by 34% by 2030 and 44% (53% including demand-side measures) by 2050 relative to 2020. Current estimates of the RCB assume strong reductions in CH4 emissions21, yet this conflicts with recent increases in CH4 emissions (following high-emission scenarios12,22,23) and only small projected near-term reductions20,24. While some have called for a separation of targets for long- and short-lived GHGs25, the required CH4 mitigation alongside CO2 mitigation for specific temperature limits remains unclear. In addition, climate targets of countries or companies are often framed as net zero CO2 or GHG emission targets, reached by linear emission reductions. This contrasts with the most prominent emission scenarios produced by the scientific community, which exhibit highly non-linear emissions pathways resulting from cost-optimization within process-based Integrated Assessment Models (IAMs)26,27,28.Here, we complement current emission scenarios by systematically quantifying how peak warming and the RCB depend on changes in CH4 emissions in scenarios with linear CO2 or GHG emission reductions, matching the dominant approach in climate policy. We provide data for setting CH4 emission targets consistent with agreed-on global climate targets, while remaining largely independent of assumptions inherent to IAM-derived scenarios. We find that without CH4 mitigation, peak warming will exceed 1.7 ∘C (50% likelihood; 1.85 ∘C with net zero CO2 emissions after 2040), and quantify how linear mid-century CH4 mitigation targets influence the RCB.Results and discussionGeneration of future emission scenariosIAMs represent important tools for informing policymaking, the climate science community, and the findings of the IPCC26,29. IAMs simulate interactions between human and physical systems to generate plausible storylines given assumptions about socioeconomic and technological developments, combined with climate-related constraints26,30. Although IAMs comprise a heterogeneous set of models, IAMs generally assume cost-effectiveness, mitigation driven by price signals, and sometimes perfect foresight26,27,28,31. Furthermore, emission scenarios are sensitive to model structure, and database statistics are strongly influenced by individual models and studies32,33.IAMs generally convert all represented GHG emissions to CO2-equivalents before global cost optimization, and thus assume similar mitigation ambition for different GHGs17,27,34. This consequential feature explains an emergent correlation between anthropogenic CO2 and CH4 emissions in IAM-generated cost-effective emission scenarios, with parts of the scenario space being undersampled (Supplementary Fig. 1). With some exceptions35, IAM-derived scenarios provide limited or no representation of CH4 mitigation due to behavioral change and technological innovation17,26. Even in strong mitigation scenarios assessed by the IPCC, CH4 emission reductions over 2019–2100 rarely exceed 50%17, often realized already around mid-century12,17. Consequently, (i) weak reductions or increases in CH4 emissions alongside net zero CO2 emissions, (ii) increased long-term CH4 mitigation potential, and (iii) economically non-optimal mitigation decisions, including the implications of politically set linear emission targets, remain largely unexplored in the emission scenarios currently in use.This way, we miss part of the possibly available and relevant scenario space for GHG mitigation, where fundamentally different combinations of CO2 and CH4 emissions can yield similar peak temperatures. Figure 1 shows an example of two idealized scenarios with (1, red) net zero CO2 emissions in 2090 combined with a 50% reduction in CH4 emissions until 2090, and (2, blue) net zero CO2 emissions in 2040 and a simultaneous increase in CH4 emissions by 20% that both peak just below 2 ∘C of warming. Notably, the peak cumulative CO2 emissions of the two scenarios differ by more than 1000 GtCO2. The red scenario aligns more with the typical outputs of IAMs, while the blue scenario lies completely outside the scenario space of the AR6 scenario database36 (Supplementary Fig. 1). We do not judge the plausibility of the two scenarios here, but note that the perceived plausibility of a future scenario is gradual and likely influenced by the dominance of economically optimal scenarios and their underlying assumptions. Given that politics in practice rarely follow cost-optimal pathways and future mitigation ambition for CO2 and CH4 may differ considerably, we argue that it is valuable to explore a more complete scenario space to quantify potential and understand the consequences of non-optimal decisions from a what-if perspective.Fig. 1: Similar peak temperature as a result of two different combinations of CO2 and CH4 emission pathways.Full size imageDifferent combinations of CO2 (a) and CH4 emission pathways (b) can lead to a similar peak global mean surface temperature (GMST) anomaly until 2100 compared to the pre-industrial period (1850–1900) (c). Shadings indicate the 33th–67th percentile and 5th–95th percentile range of the GMST anomaly. Details on the emissions of other climate forcers are provided in the Methods section.Therefore, we systematically combine different CH4 pathways with linear emission reduction trajectories from 2024 to net zero CO2 or net zero GHG emissions, while staying largely independent of the structure of IAMs (Supplementary Fig. 2). While IAMs produce emissions of climate forcers as part of their outputs, we prescribe CH4 together with either CO2 or aggregated non-CH4 GHG emissions as independent inputs. Based on these prescribed emissions, we create ensembles of compatible emissions of other climate forcers using a sectoral infilling model, relying on IAM output only for the emissions of fluorinated gases (see Methods). For each combination of emissions, we produce an ensemble of global mean surface temperature (GMST) projections with the AR6-calibrated simple climate model FaIR37,38.Peak warming in an expanded scenario spaceThis independent specification of CH4 and CO2 (or GHG) emissions enables us to expand the scenario space and explicitly show how peak GMST depends on the year of net zero CO2 or GHG emissions, respectively, and the simultaneous CH4 emission changes (Fig. 2). For a given net zero CO2 or GHG emission target year, the minimum required CH4 mitigation targets (50% likelihood) are shown in Fig. 2, and given numerically in Table 1. Analogous results for 67% likelihood can be found in Supplementary Fig. 3, and Supplementary Table 1 provides the minimum required CH4 emission targets for a 17%, 33%, 67%, and 83% likelihood of staying below a specified peak temperature.Fig. 2: Peak temperature from linear CO2 or GHG reduction pathways combined with a range of CH4 emission changes.Full size imagea The peak global mean surface temperature (GMST) anomaly until 2100 as a function of the year when net zero CO2 emissions are reached and the change in CH4 between the year 2020 and the year of net zero CO2 emissions. b The peak GMST anomaly until 2100 as a function of the year when net zero GHG emissions are reached and the change in CH4 between the year 2020 and the year of net zero GHG emissions. Both (a) and (b) show the median across the whole ensemble of simulations that includes both a spread in the inferred non-CO2, non-CH4 emissions and the climate response. Part of the shown scenario space is shaded, as no country appears to target net zero CO2 or GHG emissions before 204042,43 (considering scientific modeling conventions for emissions accounting85,86). Indicated by colored bars in (a) are the estimated CH4 mitigation at no net cost by the International Energy Agency18 (IEA) and – both assessed by the United Nations Environment Programme (UNEP) in the Global Methane Status Report 202520 – the maximum CH4 mitigation potential by 2030 with currently available measures and the change in CH4 emissions until 2050 in a current legislation scenario produced by the GAINS model56.Table 1 Minimum required CH4 emission targets relative to 2020 compatible with different peak temperatures (50% likelihood)Full size tableLimiting peak warming to 1.5 °C (50% likelihood) would require eliminating all anthropogenic CO2 and CH4 emissions until about 2028, following a linear reduction after 2024, and is therefore no longer plausible. Without CH4 mitigation, peak warming will exceed 1.7 ∘C (50% likelihood) for all net zero CO2 emission target years. Even with global net zero CO2 emissions in 2050 and a linear CO2 reduction trajectory, in the absence of CH4 mitigation, peak warming reaches almost 2 ∘C (50% likelihood). This emphasizes the need for strong, sustained CH4 reductions to limit warming to the levels of the 2015 Paris Agreement16, as also shown in earlier studies12,39,40. Given existing net zero CO2 and GHG emission targets41,42,43, the inertia in political systems, and existing and planned infrastructure44,45,46, the shaded parts of the scenario space in Fig. 2 are judged to be highly implausible, and we project peak warming of at least 1.6 ∘C even with CH4 emission reductions of 85% relative to 2020 and above 1.85 ∘C without CH4 mitigation (50% likelihood).Perhaps surprisingly, slow decarbonization can still keep warming below 2 ∘C, but only if paired with strong and sustained CH4 mitigation (2 ∘C-isoline, Fig. 2a). For example, a linear reduction in CO2 emissions reaching net zero CO2 emissions in 2100, along with a linear reduction in CH4 emissions by 83%, limits peak warming to 2 ∘C (50% likelihood). Notably, CH4 mitigation at no net cost, as estimated by the International Energy Agency (IEA)18, reduces peak warming by 0.05 ∘C. Exploiting the full near-term mitigation potential ( ~ − 32–34% by 203020) prevents around 0.15 ∘C of peak warming (Fig. 2a).Conversely, continued increases in CH4 emissions (including indirect anthropogenic and natural emissions caused by feedbacks22) lead to peak warming exceeding 2 ∘C, even with net zero CO2 emissions around mid-century or net zero GHG emissions by 2070. Following historical trends or current legislation for CH4 emissions until 205020 would increase peak warming by almost 0.15 ∘C relative to constant CH4 emissions at 2020 levels.Several countries have set mid-century net zero GHG emission targets41,42; however, peak warming still depends on CH4 mitigation stringency (Fig. 2b). Assuming an aggregation of all GHGs according to the Global Warming Potential over 100 years (GWP100) from the IPCC AR547 commonly used in national inventory reports48, and linear GHG emissions reductions, global net zero GHG emissions by 2050 yields a median peak warming of more than 1.8 ∘C (50% likelihood) without CH4 mitigation and 1.65 ∘C (50% likelihood) when 90% of anthropogenic CH4 are mitigated until 2050. For a given GHG emission pathway, absent CH4 mitigation can still increase peak temperature by up to 0.3 ∘C (besides increasing the amount of CO2 removal needed to follow a given GHG reduction pathway). This also highlights that even when considering GHGs in an aggregated manner, CH4 mitigation remains particularly important to limit global warming to 2 ∘C or less39.Uncertainty in peak warming for a prescribed combination of emission trajectories comes from (1) uncertainty in the compatible emissions of other (non-CO2, non-CH4) climate forcers (remaining scenario uncertainty), and (2) uncertainty in the climate system response to emissions (climate response uncertainty). Both depend on the location in the scenario space and generally increase with peak temperature (Supplementary Fig. 4). While the remaining scenario uncertainty ( ~ 0.1 ∘C) is influenced by the parameter ranges sampled during the infilling procedure, the overall uncertainty in the peak temperature is entirely dominated by the climate response uncertainty ( ~ 0.5 ∘C). This indicates that specifying CO2 and CH4 emission pathways eliminates most of the scenario uncertainty. Put simply, the three most important factors determining future peak global warming are (1) peak cumulative CO2 emissions, (2) future CH4 emissions, and (3) the response of the climate system to these emissions. Uncertainty in the climate system is substantial, and increasing the likelihood, for example, from 50% to 67% of staying below a specific peak temperature demands much more stringent CH4 mitigation for a given net zero CO2 or GHG emissions target (Supplementary Fig. 3 and Supplementary Table 1).The implications of linear mid-century CH4 mitigation targets for the remaining carbon budgetIn our approach, each pathway with a linear reduction of the net CO2 emissions to zero by a specific year corresponds to a maximum cumulative amount of CO2 emissions, or equivalently, a remaining carbon budget (RCB) for the given peak warming and CH4 trajectory. Fig. 3a shows the relationship between the RCBs for 1.7 ∘C and 2 ∘C (both 50% likelihood) and the (linear) change in CH4 emissions until 2050. The RCB for 2 ∘C (and generally for warming above 1.9 ∘C) is nearly linearly dependent on the mid-century CH4 emission target, suggesting a straightforward trade-off between CO2 and CH4 emissions, if net zero CO2 emissions are eventually reached: Failing to reduce CH4 emissions in 2050 by 10% compared to 2020 ( ~ 35 MtCH4/year) reduces the 2 ∘C RCB by  ~ 165 GtCO2 (5th–95th percentile: 128–225 GtCO2), equivalent to about four years of current global CO2 emissions49. This effect of CH4 mitigation on RCBs is considerably higher than previously estimated12,50, but we note that non-linear CH4 emission changes can diminish or reinforce this effect (see indicated slope of the 2 ∘C-line in Supplementary Fig. 5). While the exact size of RCBs has remaining scenario uncertainties (shading in Fig. 3a), the slope of the emerging relationship is only weakly affected. The reported trade-off between CO2 and CH4 applies specifically to peak warming in scenarios with linear changes in CH4 emissions until 2050 and net zero CO2 emissions reached later this century, which is a regime directly relevant for the design of mitigation strategies. More generally, no single conversion factor between CO2 and CH4 emissions can fully capture their different warming effects across all timescales and emission pathways due to their inherently different atmospheric lifetimes51,52.Fig. 3: The global remaining carbon budget as a function of changes in CH4 emissions between 2020 and 2050.Full size imageBoth panels show the global remaining carbon budget (RCB) at the start of 2025 for 1.7 and 2 ∘C (50% likelihood) as a function of the linear CH4 emission change until 2050. Panel a additionally shows the remaining scenario uncertainty (interquartile range and 5th–95th percentile range), and the slope of the 2 ∘C (50% likelihood) RCB with regards to the CH4 emission target for 2050. Slopes are similar for higher peak temperatures, too. The horizontal grid spacing corresponds to about five years at current CO2 emissions. Panel b includes estimates of the global RCB as presented by Lamboll et al.53, the global carbon project (GCB 2024)49, Indicators of Global Change 2024 (IGC 2024)54, and the latest IPCC Working Group 1 report (IPCC AR6)5, all updated to show the RCB as of the beginning of 2025. Horizontal error bars indicate the range of described RCB estimates, and vertical error bars refer to the changes in CH4 emissions in IAM-generated scenarios estimated in the study by Rogelj and Lamboll, 2024 (R&L 2024)21. Individual scenarios of the AR6 scenario database36 that fall within the domain of the figure are shown as black dots.A lack of near-term CH4 mitigation can lead to much earlier depletion of global RCBs: In fact, without CH4 emission reductions in 2050 relative to 2020 levels, the 1.7 ∘C RCB (50% likelihood) was already depleted before 2025. For staying below 2 ∘C (50% likelihood), less than 600 GtCO2 remain – under 15 years at current CO2 emission levels49. In principle, the RCB for 2 ∘C could also be slightly increased with strong near-term CH4 mitigation12.However, the communicated 2 ∘C RCBs (50% likelihood) are usually much higher (1015–1150 GtCO2 for 20255,49,53,54) because they implicitly include (potentially non-linear) CH4 emission reductions simulated by IAMs21. Comparing our results with current best estimates of the RCB5,49,53,54 and implied emission reductions derived by Rogelj and Lamboll21 (Fig. 3b) reveals excellent agreement regarding the 2 ∘C RCB, despite relying on a fundamentally different method for scenario generation and limiting our analysis to linear reduction in CH4 emissions. For the 1.7 ∘C RCB, we find a higher required CH4 mitigation (or equivalently a lower RCB), but agreement with previous literature improves when assuming non-linear (delayed) CO2 mitigation (Supplementary Fig. 6). Importantly, due to the correlation between CH4 and CO2 emissions in IAM-generated scenarios, the emergent structure of the covered scenario space in the AR6 scenario database36 makes it difficult to derive the dependence of RCBs on CH4 mitigation targets (black dots are individual IAM scenarios in Fig. 3b).Combined CO2 and CH4 mitigation can also be viewed through the lens of GWP*52, a GHG aggregation model that considers their different atmospheric lifetimes and the effects of changing emission rates on warming. Within the GWP* framework, decreasing CH4 emissions by  ~ 0.33% per year causes no additional warming13,55. In other words, CO2-warming-equivalent CH4 emissions are then equal to 0 t/year. With simulations using exponential CH4 emissions trajectories, we find that adopting this view results in a nearly depleted RCB for 1.7 ∘C and a 2 ∘C RCB of only 750 (5th–95th percentile: 290–1230) GtCO2 (50% likelihood, Supplementary Fig. 5).ConclusionHere we systematically quantify how peak warming and RCBs depend on the stringency of CH4 mitigation. Our approach complements IAMs by expanding the explored scenario space outside economically optimal, GWP100-aggregated emission trajectories, revealing structures and trade-offs not apparent in standard scenario databases. Importantly, our findings add to IAM-based conclusions instead of contradicting them: our calculated CH4 reductions implied by existing RCB estimates align closely with previous point estimates derived from IAM-based emission scenarios. Except for the illustrative case of exponential changes in CH4 emissions, we limit ourselves to simple linear emission pathways starting from 2024 for net CO2 and CH4 emissions, while IAMs often output non-linear emission trajectories. Although this limits comparability, policymakers have so far preferred linear target setting, which we intend to mimic with our emission scenarios. Other shapes of emission trajectories could, of course, be explored with the described approach for scenario generation.The broader, so far unexplored perspective on the scenario space matters because climate policy rarely follows least-cost optimization alone. Political and social feasibility, institutional constraints, and implementation timelines also influence the stringency of CO2 and CH4 mitigation. CH4 mitigation is compelling precisely because it aligns multiple objectives: it is technically feasible with known and untapped potential12,18,20,56, economically attractive with national benefits even without global cooperation57,58, and affects global temperatures in the near-term by slowing down warming or even leading to slight interim cooling. Yet, CH4 mitigation remains underfunded59 and many emission sources are not covered by policies12. Even highly cost-effective measures, such as leak repair, are often not realized, due to a misalignment of incentives (e.g., regulatory regimes that allow gas distribution firms to pass the costs of leaked gas on to customers60), competing investment priorities, and weak regulatory pressure12,18.Our results underscore both the opportunity and urgency of taking action on CH4 emissions. Realizing the near-term CH4 mitigation potential could alone prevent around 0.15 ∘C of warming this century and grant us additional flexibility in the timeline of decarbonization. Conversely, without stringent CH4 mitigation, limiting warming below 2 ∘C becomes unlikely even with extremely ambitious CO2 emission reductions. The RCB is, to some degree, influenced by CH4 mitigation, but since current total anthropogenic CH4 emissions are finite, there is a physical limit to how much RCBs can be expanded. We would like to emphasize that RCBs are in fact smaller than commonly presented in previous literature5,49,53,54 and to policymakers1, if CH4 emissions do not fall as implicitly assumed21,61. In any case, CH4 mitigation cannot substitute for achieving net zero CO2 emissions1,12, and certain impacts of delayed CO2 mitigation are unaffected by CH4 mitigation, like ocean acidification. Our focus is on the effect of sustained changes in CH4 emissions in the context of scenarios that reach net zero CO2 or net zero GHG emissions this century, followed by net negative CO2 or GHG emissions. The results and conclusions presented, therefore, depend on reducing CO2 emissions. Put differently, only if net zero CO2 emissions are achieved can the benefit of CH4 mitigation on peak warming be realized62.The purpose of models extends beyond prediction to expanding our understanding of system dynamics and revealing the consequences of choices. Analyzing vast scenario spaces leads to the emergence of patterns and uncovers prerequisites of actions. While IAM-based scenario databases address many policy-relevant questions30, complementary approaches are needed for others, such as exploring the consequences of non-optimal decisions, and mapping and communicating the structure of the available (and rapidly narrowing) mitigation space. To support policymakers’ decisions, we provide specific minimum CH4 emission targets to complement existing net zero CO2 or GHG emission targets. Keeping global warming to below 2 ∘C requires CH4 mitigation to become a core element of any credible mitigation strategy.MethodsSystematic generation of emission scenariosWe generate a suite of simple emission scenarios by systematically combining linear emission trajectories for CH4 with linear reduction pathways for net CO2 or GHG emissions. Using the simple climate model FaIR37,63 version 2.1.3 with the AR6-consistent calibration v1.4.138, we generate ensemble projections of the resulting global mean surface temperature (GMST) until 2200. FaIR was one of the three simple climate models used in the IPCC AR6 WGIII29 to assess the temperature outcomes of submitted emissions scenarios and is calibrated to the latest generation of Earth System Models38. FaIR and its calibration account for all major anthropogenic and natural forcings, including global effects of aerosols, albedo change due to land use, and prescribed solar and volcanic forcing37,38. Consistent with calibration v1.4.1, contrail forcing is not considered38.We use historical emissions from ScenarioMIP64 up to the year 2024. Constructed emission scenarios diverge in 2025; however, our modeling approach could be updated annually with the latest emission data. We prescribe either net anthropogenic CO2 emissions or net anthropogenic GHG emissions with linear emission trajectories between 2024 and years of net zero emissions extend from 2025 to 2100 at five-year intervals (16 different pathways). Net CO2/GHG emission pathways following net zero CO2/GHG emissions are varied by sampling different maximum net negative CO2 or GHG emissions and net negative realization factors, as described in Section Monte Carlo Simulations (see also Supplementary Table 2), and are therefore included in the scenario uncertainty.We consider three types of anthropogenic CH4 emission trajectories:
                  
                    Linear changes between 2024 and the year of net zero CO2 or net zero GHG emissions, ranging from -90% to +50% relative to 2020 CH4 emissions at an increment of 5% (29 scenarios) and constant emissions afterward, used for the analysis of the expanded scenario space.
                  
                  
                    Linear changes between 2024 and 2050, ranging from -90% to +50% relative to 2020 CH4 emissions at an increment of 5% (29 scenarios) and constant emissions afterward (only combined with net CO2 emission pathways), used for calculations of the RCB.
                  
                  
                    Exponential changes starting from 2024 CH4 emissions, ranging between -6%/year and +1.5%/year at an increment of 0.25%/year (31 scenarios, only combined with net CO2 emission pathways), used to assess the implications for the RCB when assuming no additional warming from CH4 emissions under the GWP* model.
                  
                Only direct anthropogenic sources of CH4 emissions are included: fossil fuel production, agriculture, waste management, and anthropogenic biomass burning. Still, prescribed future changes in CH4 emissions can be conceived as the combined change in anthropogenic and natural emissions, including increases in natural CH4 emissions through feedback processes.Model structure for infilling of other emissionsThe emissions of the other (non-CO2, non-CH4) climate forcers are inferred based on prescribed net CO2 and CH4 emissions and a set of 21 model parameters (Supplementary Fig. 2). When net GHG emissions are prescribed, net CO2 emissions are calculated first, as described below in Section Workflow for linear GHG emission pathways. The climate forcers to be inferred (or “infilled”) comprise seven short-lived climate forcers (SLCFs: black carbon aerosols (BC), carbon monoxide (CO), ammonia (NH3), non-methane volatile organic compounds (NMVOC), nitrogen oxides (NOx), organic carbon aerosols (OC), and sulfur dioxide (SO2)), nitrous oxide (N2O), and 40 species of fluorinated gases (F-gases). For each combination of prescribed emissions, we calculate combinations of consistent emissions pathways for these climate forcers. For example, certain air pollutants (such as SO2, BC, and NOx) are co-emitted with CO2, thus reaching net zero CO2 emissions will lead to reductions in their emissions, too. However, there exists no unique mapping from prescribed to infilled emissions to ensure consistency of infilled with prescribed emission trajectories, but rather a range of plausible input assumptions that lead to different sets of infilled emissions. With the infilling model described in the following, we aim to remain sufficiently flexible in covering the space of consistent emission trajectories dependent on an interpretable set of parameters. We use Monte Carlo sampling to create sets of approximately consistent emission pathways based on different parameter combinations for any combination of prescribed net CO2 and CH4 emission pathways.Inferring gross fossil CO2 emissionsFirst, prescribed net CO2 emissions are split into net fossil CO2 emissions (\({E}_{{{{\rm{CO}}}}_{2}}^{{{\rm{FFI,net}}}}\)) and net CO2 emissions from agriculture, forestry, and other land use (\({E}_{{{{\rm{CO}}}}_{2}}^{{{\rm{AFOLU,net}}}}\)) according to their relative shares in 2024 and both reaching net zero emissions in the specified net zero CO2 emission year on a linear trajectory. To calculate gross fossil CO2 emissions (\({E}_{{{{\rm{CO}}}}_{2}}^{{{\rm{FFI}}},{{\rm{gross}}}}\)) from \({E}_{{{{\rm{CO}}}}_{2}}^{{{\rm{FFI,net}}}}\), we allow for two functional forms that can both be described by a single parameter: the residual CO2 emissions at net zero CO2 emissions (\({E}_{{{{\rm{CO}}}}_{2}}^{{{{\rm{res,netzeroCO}}}}_{2}}\)). The first functional form is simply a lower bound for \({E}_{{{{\rm{CO}}}}_{2}}^{{{\rm{FFI}}},{{\rm{gross}}}}\): $$\begin{array}{rcl}&&\,{\mbox{Functional}}\,\,\,{\mbox{form}}\,\,1\,({\mbox{bound}})\!:\\ {E}_{{{{\rm{CO}}}}_{2}}^{{{\rm{FFI}}},{{\rm{gross}}}}(t)&=&\left\{\begin{array}{ll}{E}_{{{{\rm{CO}}}}_{2}}^{{{\rm{FFI}}},{{\rm{net}}}}(t)\quad \hfill &\,{{\mbox{if}}}\,\,{E}_{{{{\rm{CO}}}}_{2}}^{{{\rm{FFI}}},{{\rm{net}}}}(t) > {E}_{{{{\rm{CO}}}}_{2}}^{{{\rm{res}}},{{{\rm{netzeroCO}}}}_{2}}\\ {E}_{{{{\rm{CO}}}}_{2}}^{{{\rm{res}}},{{{\rm{netzeroCO}}}}_{2}}\quad &\,{{\mbox{if}}}\,\,{E}_{{{{\rm{CO}}}}_{2}}^{{{\rm{FFI}}},\,{{\rm{net}}}}(t)\le {E}_{{{{\rm{CO}}}}_{2}}^{{{\rm{res}}},{{{\rm{netzeroCO}}}}_{2}}\end{array}\right.\end{array}$$
                    (1)
                The second functional represents a smoothed relationship between \({{{\rm{CO}}}}_{2}^{{{\rm{FFI}}},{{\rm{gross}}}}\) and \({{{\rm{CO}}}}_{2}^{{{\rm{FFI}}},{{\rm{net}}}}\) (\({R}_{{{{\rm{CO}}}}_{2}}^{{{\rm{net}}}\to {{\rm{gross}}}}\)) of the AR6 scenario database36 (Supplementary Fig. 7). This way, the shape of the relationship is informed by the output of IAMs; however, the amount of \({{{\rm{CO}}}}_{2}^{{{\rm{FFI}}},{{\rm{gross}}}}\) for different \({{{\rm{CO}}}}_{2}^{{{\rm{FFI}}},{{\rm{net}}}}\) is controlled by \({{{\rm{CO}}}}_{2}^{{{\rm{res}}},{{{\rm{netzeroCO}}}}_{2}}\) through a scaling factor (fsmoothed) and hence not influenced by the summary statistics of the AR6 scenario database.$$\begin{array}{rcl}&&\,{\mbox{Functional}}\,\,{{\mbox{form}}}\,2\,({{\mbox{smoothed}}})\!: \hfill \\ {E}_{{{{\rm{CO}}}}_{2}}^{{{\rm{FFI}}},{{\rm{gross}}}}(t)&=&{R}_{{{{\rm{CO}}}}_{2}}^{{{\rm{net}}}\to {{\rm{gross}}}}({E}_{{{{\rm{CO}}}}_{2}}^{{{\rm{FFI}}},{{\rm{net}}}}(t),{E}_{{{{\rm{CO}}}}_{2}}^{{{\rm{res}}},{{{\rm{netzeroCO}}}}_{2}})\hfill\end{array}$$
                    (2)
                Infilling model for short-lived climate forcers and N2OFor these eight species (seven SLCFs and N2O), we distinguish between emissions from fossil, industrial, and agricultural sources, and emissions from biomass burning. Fossil, industrial, and agricultural emissions are modeled using sector-specific emission factors, assumptions about their changes, and the Community Earth atmospheric Data System (CEDS) v_2025_03_18 Aggregate Data65,66 (an earlier version of the same dataset was used in the calibration of FaIR38). We separate the 62 sectors represented in CEDS into sets (denoted as σ) of sectors where (a) CO2 and CH4 are co-emitted (\(| {\sigma }_{{{{\rm{CO}}}}_{2},{{{\rm{CH}}}}_{4}}| =33\)), (b) CO2 but no CH4 is emitted (\(| {\sigma }_{{{{\rm{CO}}}}_{2}}| =10\)), (c) CH4 but no CO2 is emitted (\(| {\sigma }_{{{{\rm{CH}}}}_{4}}| =7\)), and (d) neither CO2 nor CH4 is emitted (∣σsep∣ = 12) in 2023. We also use the following sectoral categories to group sectors inspired by McDuffie et al.67 (number of sector in brackets, see Supplementary Table 3): Energy production (10), Industry (27), Transportation (4), Residential (3), Solvents (4), Agriculture (5), Waste (4), Shipping (2), Aviation (2), Indirect non-agricultural N2O (1). The emissions of a species \(s\in \left\{{{\rm{BC}}},{{\rm{CO}}},{{{\rm{NH}}}}_{3},{{\rm{NMVOC}}},{{{\rm{NO}}}}_{x},{{\rm{OC}}},{{{\rm{SO}}}}_{2},{{{\rm{N}}}}_{2}{{\rm{O}}}\right\}\) in the sectors covered by CEDS are then decomposed into (variables explained below): $${E}_{s}^{{{\rm{CEDS}}}}(t) = 	 {\sum} _{i\in {\sigma }_{{{{\rm{CO}}}}_{2},{{{\rm{CH}}}}_{4}}}\left[{f}_{s}^{i,{{{\rm{CO}}}}_{2}}(t)\cdot {E}_{{{{\rm{CO}}}}_{2}}^{{{\rm{FFI}}},{{\rm{gross}}}}(t)\cdot {\rho }_{{{{\rm{CO}}}}_{2}}^{i}(t)\cdot {w}^{i}\right.\\ 	 \left.+{f}_{s}^{i,{{{\rm{CH}}}}_{4}}(t)\cdot {E}_{{{{\rm{CH}}}}_{4}}(t)\cdot {\rho }_{{{{\rm{CH}}}}_{4}}^{i}(t)\cdot \left(1-{w}^{i}\right)\right]\\ 	 + {\sum} _{j\in {\sigma }_{{{{\rm{CO}}}}_{2}}}{f}_{s}^{j,{{{\rm{CO}}}}_{2}}(t)\cdot {E}_{{{{\rm{CO}}}}_{2}}^{{{\rm{FFI}}},{{\rm{gross}}}}(t)\cdot {\rho }_{{{{\rm{CO}}}}_{2}}^{j}(t)\\ 	 +{\sum} _{k\in {\sigma }_{{{{\rm{CH}}}}_{4}}}{f}_{s}^{k,{{{\rm{CH}}}}_{4}}(t)\cdot {E}_{{{{\rm{CH}}}}_{4}}(t)\cdot {\rho }_{{{{\rm{CH}}}}_{4}}^{k}(t)\\ 	 + {\sum}_{l\in {\sigma }_{{{\rm{sep}}}}}{E}_{s}^{l}(t)$$
                    (3)
                In Equation (3), \({f}_{s}^{x,{{{\rm{CO}}}}_{2}}(t)\) and \({f}_{s}^{x,{{{\rm{CH}}}}_{4}}(t)\) denote the emission of species s in sector x per emission of CO2 and CH4 in sector x, respectively, and can be conceptualized as sector-specific relative emission factors. If species s is not emitted in a sector x, then \({f}_{s}^{x,{{{\rm{CO}}}}_{2}}(t)={f}_{s}^{x,{{{\rm{CH}}}}_{4}}(t)=0\). Emission factors relative to CH4 are assumed to be constant and taken from CEDS data averaged over a reference time period τref.$${f}_{s}^{x,{{{\rm{CH}}}}_{4}}(t)=\frac{{E}_{s}^{x}(t)}{{E}_{{{{\rm{CH}}}}_{4}}^{x}(t)}\approx \frac{{E}_{s}^{x}({\tau }_{{{\rm{ref}}}})}{{E}_{{{{\rm{CH}}}}_{4}}^{x}({\tau }_{{{\rm{ref}}}})}$$
                    (4)
                Because there is a history of regulating combustion-related emissions of air pollutants and decoupling them from CO2 emissions11,68,69, we include the option of \({f}_{s}^{x,{{{\rm{CO}}}}_{2}}(t)\) for the seven SLCFs in the sectoral categories Energy production, Industry, Transportation, Residential, and Waste to decrease over time70,71,72. We calculate regionally disaggregated sector-specific relative emission factors for eight world regions (aggregation taken from the Global Carbon Budget 202449) and include the option for \({f}_{s}^{x,{{{\rm{CO}}}}_{2}}(t)\) to linearly converge to the regional and sector minimum \({f}_{s}^{x,{{{\rm{CO}}}}_{2,\min }}({\tau }_{{{\rm{ref}}}})\) by a target year tap.$${f}_{s}^{x,{{{\rm{CO}}}}_{2}}(t)=\frac{{E}_{s}^{x}(t)}{{E}_{{{{\rm{CO}}}}_{2}}^{x}(t)}\approx \left\{\begin{array}{ll}\frac{{E}_{s}^{x}({\tau }_{{{\rm{ref}}}})}{{E}_{{{{\rm{CO}}}}_{2}}^{x}({\tau }_{{{\rm{ref}}}})}\quad\hfill &{{\rm{if}}}\,{{\rm{no}}}\,{{\rm{additional}}}\,{{\rm{air}}}\,{{\rm{pollution}}}\,{{\rm{measures}}}\hfill\\ \frac{{E}_{s}^{x}({\tau }_{{{\rm{ref}}}})}{{E}_{{{{\rm{CO}}}}_{2}}^{x}({\tau }_{{{\rm{ref}}}})}\cdot (1-p(t))+{f}_{s}^{x,{{{\rm{CO}}}}_{2,\min }}({\tau }_{{{\rm{ref}}}})\cdot p(t)\quad &{{\rm{if}}}\,{{\rm{additional}}}\,{{\rm{air}}}\,{{\rm{pollution}}}\,{{\rm{measures}}}\,{{\rm{for}}}\,s,\,{{\rm{and}}}\,x\,{{\rm{in}}}\,{{\rm{affected}}}\,{{\rm{sectoral}}}\,{{\rm{category}}}\end{array}\right.$$
                    (5)
                The factor r changes linearly from 2024 to the target year tap: $$p(t)=\min \left(1,\frac{t-2024}{{t}_{{{\rm{ap}}}}-2024}\right)$$
                    (6)
                In Equation (3), \({\rho }_{{{{\rm{CO}}}}_{2}}^{x}(t)\) denotes the share of (total) gross fossil CO2 emissions that occur in sector x and equivalently \({\rho }_{{{{\rm{CH}}}}_{4}}^{x}(t)\) denotes the share of (total) CH4 emissions that occur in sector x. These shares can either be chosen to be fixed (constant sectoral split) or change linearly until net zero CO2/GHG emissions are reached to account for differences in sectoral composition between current and residual emissions35,73,74. This does not impact the prescribed CO2 or CH4 emissions, but changes the composition of co-emitted species that are infilled over time. To reduce the number of input parameters, we fix the relative contributions to total emissions of CO2 and CH4 within the different sectoral categories (\({\rho }_{{{{\rm{CO}}}}_{2}}^{x| C}({\tau }_{{{\rm{ref}}}})\) and \({\rho }_{{{{\rm{CH}}}}_{4}}^{x| C}({\tau }_{{{\rm{ref}}}})\), respectively). Therefore, only the shares of the different sectoral categories at net zero CO2/GHG emissions for CO2 (\({\rho }_{{{{\rm{CO}}}}_{2}}^{C,{{\rm{netzero}}}}\), 8 relevant sectoral categories) and CH4 (\({\rho }_{{{{\rm{CH}}}}_{4}}^{C,{{\rm{netzero}}}}\), 3 relevant sectoral categories) need specification (Supplementary Table 2).$${\rho }_{{{{\rm{CO}}}}_{2}}^{x}(t)=\frac{{E}_{{{{\rm{CO}}}}_{2}}^{x}(t)}{{E}_{{{{\rm{CO}}}}_{2}}^{{{\rm{FFI}}},{{\rm{gross}}}}(t)}\approx \left\{\begin{array}{ll}\frac{{E}_{{{{\rm{CO}}}}_{2}}^{x}({\tau }_{{{\rm{ref}}}})}{{E}_{{{{\rm{CO}}}}_{2}}^{{{\rm{FFI}}},{{\rm{gross}}}}({\tau }_{{{\rm{ref}}}})}\quad &\,{\mbox{if split = const.}}\,\\ \frac{{E}_{{{{\rm{CO}}}}_{2}}^{x}({\tau }_{{{\rm{ref}}}})}{{E}_{{{{\rm{CO}}}}_{2}}^{{{\rm{FFI}}},{{\rm{gross}}}}({\tau }_{{{\rm{ref}}}})}\cdot (1-q(t))+{\rho }_{{{{\rm{CO}}}}_{2}}^{C,{{\rm{netzero}}}}\cdot {\rho }_{{{{\rm{CO}}}}_{2}}^{x| C}({\tau }_{{{\rm{ref}}}})\cdot q(t)\quad &\,{\mbox{otherwise}}\,\end{array}\right.$$
                    (7)
                $${\rho }_{{{{\rm{CH}}}}_{4}}^{x}(t)=\frac{{E}_{{{{\rm{CH}}}}_{4}}^{x}(t)}{{E}_{{{{\rm{CH}}}}_{4}}(t)}\approx \left\{\begin{array}{ll}\frac{{E}_{{{{\rm{CH}}}}_{4}}^{x}({\tau }_{{{\rm{ref}}}})}{{E}_{{{{\rm{CH}}}}_{4}}({\tau }_{{{\rm{ref}}}})}\quad \hfill&\,{\mbox{if split = const.}}\,\\ \frac{{E}_{{{{\rm{CH}}}}_{4}}^{x}({\tau }_{{{\rm{ref}}}})}{{E}_{{{{\rm{CH}}}}_{4}}({\tau }_{{{\rm{ref}}}})}\cdot (1-q(t))+{\rho }_{{{{\rm{CH}}}}_{4}}^{C,{{\rm{netzero}}}}\cdot {\rho }_{{{{\rm{CH}}}}_{4}}^{x| C}({\tau }_{{{\rm{ref}}}})\cdot q(t)\quad &\,{\mbox{otherwise}}\,\end{array}\right.$$
                    (8)
                 The factor q changes linearly between 2024 and the year of net zero CO2/GHG emissions (tnetzero): $$q(t)=\min \left(1,\frac{t-2024}{{t}_{{{\rm{netzero}}}}-2024}\right)$$
                    (9)
                For sectors resolved in CEDS where CO2 and CH4 are co-emitted, the emissions of species s depend on both prescribed CO2 and CH4 emissions in our model. This requires attributing changes in s separately to CO2 and CH4 emissions. To account for different relative influences on co-emitted species, we introduce a (sector-dependent) weighting factor (wi). We choose to make the relative influence of CO2 emissions on emissions of all infilled species in sector i, and hence wi, proportional to \({\rho }_{{{{\rm{CO}}}}_{2}}^{i}({\tau }_{{{\rm{ref}}}})\) (the contribution of sector i to total gross fossil CO2 emissions in the reference period): $${w}^{i}=\frac{{\rho }_{{{{\rm{CO}}}}_{2}}^{i}({\tau }_{{{\rm{ref}}}})}{{\rho }_{{{{\rm{CO}}}}_{2}}^{i}({\tau }_{{{\rm{ref}}}})+{\rho }_{{{{\rm{CH}}}}_{4}}^{i}({\tau }_{{{\rm{ref}}}})}$$
                    (10)
                For the emissions of s in sectors where neither CO2 nor CH4 are emitted, we assume constant emissions taken from the reference time period τref.$${E}_{s}^{l}(t)={E}_{s}^{l}({\tau }_{{{\rm{ref}}}})\,\,{\mbox{for}}\,\,l\in {\sigma }_{{{\rm{sep}}}}$$
                    (11)
                Future emissions of SLCFs and N2O from biomass burning heavily depend on a range of anthropogenic factors, such as (changes in) land use and fire management11, overlaid with a general increased risk of fire with higher global warming75,76. Emissions from biomass burning are hence highly uncertain11. Importantly, there is no simple way of constraining them for a combination of prescribed global net CO2 and CH4 emission pathways, and we therefore allow for maximum flexibility in our infilling model. We use global mean emission data up to 2022 from the beta version of the Global Fire Emissions Database (GFED) version 577 (downloaded from https://surfdrive.surf.nl/files/index.php/s/VPMEYinPeHtWVxn?path=%2FGFED5_Beta_summary_tables) averaged over a reference time period τref,bb and let emissions linearly increase or decrease until 2100 (stable afterwards) relative to τref,bb by a factor Φbb, which needs to be specified. An earlier version of GFED was used in the calibration of FaIR38.$${E}_{s}^{{{\rm{bb}}}}(t)\approx {E}_{s}^{{{\rm{bb}}}}({\tau }_{{{\rm{ref}}},{{\rm{bb}}}})\cdot (1-r(t))+(1+{\Phi }_{{{\rm{bb}}}})\cdot {E}_{s}^{{{\rm{bb}}}}({\tau }_{{{\rm{ref}}},{{\rm{bb}}}})\cdot r(t)$$
                    (12)
                $$r(t)=\min \left(1,\frac{t-2024}{2100-2024}\right)$$
                    (13)
                Finally, we add the two contributions and harmonize them with historical emissions to avoid jumps in emissions between 2024 and 2025. Post-2024 raw infilled emissions of s (\({E}_{s}^{{{\rm{raw}}}}(t)\)) are scaled according to the relative deviation between calculated and historical total emissions in 2024 to obtain the final infilled emissions (\({E}_{s}^{{{\rm{infilled}}}}(t)\)): $${E}_{s}^{{{\rm{raw}}}}(t)={E}_{s}^{{{\rm{CEDS}}}}(t)+{E}_{s}^{{{\rm{bb}}}}(t)$$
                    (14)
                $${E}_{s}^{{{\rm{infilled}}}}(t)={E}_{s}^{{{\rm{raw}}}}(t)\cdot \frac{{E}_{s}^{{{\rm{hist}}}}(2024)}{{E}_{s}^{{{\rm{raw}}}}(2024)}$$
                    (15)
                Infilling of F-gasesWe model emissions of F-gases as exogenously driven and independent of the prescribed combination of CO2 and CH4 emissions. Emissions of F-gases are linked to continuous or end-of-life leakage from equipment, and a few specialized industry sectors78,79. Their mitigation is subject to targeted legislation80,81, which is independent of the mitigation of CO2 and CH4 emissions. To fill in missing F-gas emissions, we use data from the IAM-derived shared socioeconomic pathway (SSP) scenarios82,83 provided and extended in the used distribution of FaIR37,38 to project their future emissions. This remains the only place where we explicitly rely on output from IAMs. Dependent on the species, we either interpolate linearly between historical and 2030 emissions or scale all future emissions to have consistency in 2024 emission levels (in case of strong deviation between SSPs and historical emissions until 2024, see Supplementary Table 4).Scenario for Fig. 1For the emissions scenarios in Fig. 1, we cap net negative CO2 emissions at  − 2 GtCO2/year, with the slope of the net fossil CO2 emissions halving after reaching net zero CO2 emissions. \({E}_{{{{\rm{CO}}}}_{2}}^{{{\rm{FFI}}},{{\rm{gross}}}}(t)\) are calculated using the smoothed functional form (Equation (2) with \({E}_{{{{\rm{CO}}}}_{2}}^{{{{\rm{res,netzeroCO}}}}_{2}}=6\) GtCO2/year (fsmoothed = 0.312). Furthermore, τref is 2021-2023, \({f}_{s}^{x,{{{\rm{CO}}}}_{2}}(t)\), \({\rho }_{s}^{x,{{{\rm{CO}}}}_{2}}(t)\) and \({\rho }_{s}^{x,{{{\rm{CH}}}}_{4}}(t)\) are set to be constant (no additional air pollution measures and constant sectoral split), \({E}_{s}^{{{\rm{bb}}}}(t)\) are set to be stable with τref,bb from 2003-2022. Emissions of F-gases are taken from SSP2-4.582.Workflow for linear GHG emission pathwaysIn the case of combining different prescribed CH4 emissions pathways with linear net GHG emissions pathways, we iteratively calculate the proper net CO2 emission pathways for each given CH4 emission pathway. We start by initializing N2O emissions as constant from the last historical year and filling in F-gases. For each year, CH4, N2O, and F-gas emissions are aggregated according to the chosen metric (e.g., GWP100 AR547) and an initial net CO2 emission estimate is obtained as the difference to the prescribed net GHG emission pathway. Based on the CH4 emission pathway and the net CO2 emission estimate, we update N2O emissions and SLCFs using the infilling model described above. We repeat the recalculation of net CO2 emissions and infilling of N2O and SLCFs until the aggregated GHG emission pathway deviates from the linear one by less than 0.1 MtCO2eq/year in all years.Monte Carlo simulationsWe propagate the uncertainty in the parameters of the infilling model using Monte Carlo Sampling and generate 2000 different emission scenarios for each combination of net zero CO2/GHG target year and an accompanying CH4 pathway. There are a total of 21 parameters that control the net negative CO2/GHG emissions after the year of net zero emissions and the infilling of non-CO2, non-CH4 climate forcers. 19 of 21 parameters are sampled from truncated Gaussian, uniform, or categorical distributions reflecting ranges from the assessed literature, and two parameters are fixed (Supplementary Table 2). We note that when setting parameter values and ranges, it remains difficult to stay completely independent of IAMs, as our perception of plausible parameter values is likely influenced by literature explicitly using IAMs or implicitly relying on their results. More detail on the chosen parameter ranges is given in the Supplementary Information (Supplementary Note: Monte Carlo parameter sampling).

Multilayer soil moisture depletion intensifies drought impacts on global ecosystems
                        Xihui Gu 
            ORCID: orcid.org/0000-0002-7414-53711,2,3, Ruijie Wang 
            ORCID: orcid.org/0009-0003-2345-95431, Deliang Chen4,5, Chiyuan Miao 
            ORCID: orcid.org/0000-0001-6413-70206, Sijia Luo1, Yansong Guan 
            ORCID: orcid.org/0000-0002-0048-62537, Sixiang Wang1, Liangwei Li 
            ORCID: orcid.org/0009-0001-2658-10801, Tianshun Gu

AbstractWhen soil moisture across all layers of the entire profile is depleted, ecosystems face the highest risk because they lose all vertical buffering capacity against drought. However, these vertically compound soil moisture droughts, in which every soil layer suffers simultaneous water deficits, have been largely ignored because previous monitoring and risk assessments relied on entire-profile mean soil moisture. Here we identify vertically (0–100 cm) compound droughts worldwide during warm seasons of 1981–2020 using multilayer soil moisture products. Their annual duration and ratio have increased across more than half of global lands over the past four decades, with pronounced hotspots in southwestern North America, South America, Africa, mid-latitude Eurasia, southeastern Asia and Australia. Vertically compound droughts cause substantial declines in ecosystem productivity, particularly in forests and croplands, threatening carbon sink stability and food security. By contrast, diagnosing drought solely from entire-profile averages causes an overestimation of vertically compound drought duration by about 128.3% but an underestimation of associated ecosystem losses by about 27.8%. These projections and systematic biases highlight the urgency of developing multilayer monitoring, mitigation and adaptation strategies for vertically compound droughts.
